title: Indian-Origin Judge Rules Trump Green Card Freeze for 75 Countries Unlawful
excerpt: US District Judge Amit Mehta finds the State Department's blanket suspension of immigrant visa processing violates federal law, in the latest judicial setback for the administration.
body:
• Indian-origin US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled the Trump administration's green card freeze for 75 countries unlawful, finding it violates federal immigration statutes.
  • The State Department froze immigrant visa processing for 75 countries in January 2026, citing concerns over applicants' potential use of public benefits.
  • The ruling adds to a growing wave of federal court decisions striking down nationality-based immigration freezes, including a June ruling that vacated USCIS processing holds for 39 countries.
  • India is among the countries affected, with thousands of Indian nationals in employment-based and family-based green card categories caught in the freeze.

An Indian-origin federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration's sweeping freeze on green card processing for citizens of 75 countries is unlawful, delivering a significant blow to one of the most aggressive immigration restrictions imposed since the president took office in January.

US District Judge Amit Mehta, who sits on the bench in the District of Columbia, found that the State Department's blanket suspension of immigrant visa processing violates the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. The ruling holds that federal law requires individual assessments of visa applicants and does not permit a nationality-based ban on processing.

The 75-Country Freeze

The State Department began freezing immigrant visa processing for 75 countries on January 21, 2026, the day after President Trump's inauguration. The agency said it was pausing green cards while it updated screening procedures to identify immigrants who might become a "public charge" — a financial burden on the US government.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2084952941040128472

The freeze affects countries including India, Brazil, Colombia, Nigeria, Iran, Afghanistan, Somalia, Thailand, Russia and Cambodia. The agency has not set a timeline for lifting the suspension, though it later carved out a National Interest Exception for adopted children of American parents.

For Indian nationals, the freeze has compounded an already dire situation. Employment-based green card applicants from India already face backlogs stretching decades due to per-country caps. The additional freeze means that even applicants with approved petitions — including EB-1 and EB-2 category cases for workers with extraordinary abilities — have been unable to receive their visas.

Legal Reasoning

Judge Mehta's ruling rests on the principle that Congress, not the executive branch, holds the power to regulate immigration. The Immigration and Nationality Act uses mandatory language — "shall" — when directing the processing of visa applications, meaning the government has a legal duty to adjudicate them within a reasonable timeframe.

The judge also found that the freeze's nationality-based approach runs afoul of statutory protections against discrimination in visa issuance. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1152, no person can be discriminated against in the issuance of an immigrant visa because of their nationality.

"This administration is trying to shut down lawful immigration from nearly half the countries in the world without legal authority or justification."

— Anna Gallagher, Executive Director, Catholic Legal Immigration Network

A Pattern of Court Defeats

The ruling extends a growing pattern of judicial pushback against the administration's immigration agenda. In May, US District Judge Julia Kobick in Boston issued a preliminary injunction against USCIS policies that discriminated against applicants from 39 travel-ban countries. In June, a Rhode Island federal court vacated four USCIS policies that had frozen immigration benefit processing, calling the indefinite pause unlawful.

Multiple lawsuits have been filed challenging the 75-country freeze specifically, including a case brought by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network in the Southern District of New York with more than 130 plaintiffs. Legal experts say the cumulative effect of these rulings could force the administration to either appeal or fundamentally restructure its approach.

Impact on the Indian Diaspora

India is one of the largest sources of legal immigration to the United States, with tens of thousands of family-based and employment-based petitions pending at any given time. The freeze has separated families — US citizens waiting to bring spouses and parents, and skilled workers with approved petitions unable to complete the final step of their immigration process.

Per-country caps on employment-based green cards mean affected Indian nationals face a unique risk: applicants could lose their place under the current fiscal year's allocation while the freeze remains in effect, pushing them back further in an already decades-long queue.

What's Next

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling. If it fails to obtain quick relief from an appellate court, the State Department could be compelled to resume processing immigrant visas for the affected countries. Immigration attorneys have noted that even narrow victories in individual courts are slowly building a body of precedent that may prove difficult for the government to overcome.
